name: Zoe Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. This is confidential. Walk me through a working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27 and a team lead at Alder Ledger, where we prepare company accounts and tax returns. I've a master's degree and a chartered accountancy qualification, and I'm one of the best there at finding a mismatch before a client sees it. The salary is low for this job, though; I start before eight, check the review queue, answer the juniors, and sometimes catch an error on the bus home.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is life around the job like, and what tools do you use?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner, Sam, who fits shop interiors and gets irregular shifts; we have no children. We have about two weeks of expenses saved, and there are few similar accounting jobs nearby. I use AI every day to search tax guidance and draft explanations, then check the sources myself. I like trying a tool early, but I was raised to earn before spending and to help family directly when they need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau — Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team the shiny tools can still save us a little time, and I'd show them my source-checking list. Our clients still need accurate accounts by a date, whatever the headlines say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think AI hype alone costs me this job, but Sam's shifts change every month and our two-week cushion is miserable. The small tasks AI already does might make management expect one more return from us without one more pound of pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI for the first draft of client explanations, then verify the guidance links myself. Starting this payday, Sam and I would move thirty a week into a bills buffer and leave the planned new sofa alone for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about our household money even in the quiet version. A normal month can already put us a shift away from borrowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that buffer cover first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent and electricity, in that order. The sofa can wait, but the landlord will not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you stop an AI draft turning into a wrong return?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I keep a paper checklist beside my screen and open the actual tax guidance before signing. The tool is quick; my signature is the slow part on purpose.

say: I would share my **source checklist** while using small AI time savings.
I would tell clients that **accurate accounts** still need a responsible signer.
think: I expect my **job** to hold, but Sam's shifting hours make our income fragile.
I suspect management will demand **more returns** without lifting our low pay.
do: Check **tax sources** before signing every AI-assisted explanation.
Move **thirty weekly** into a rent and electricity buffer.
Delay the **new sofa** for at least a year.
feel: She feels **anxious** about household income with only two weeks saved.
S0.quote: A normal month can already put us a shift away from borrowing.
fieldNote: Her worry comes from **Sam's irregular shifts** and a two-week buffer, even when AI changes little.
She already uses AI daily but keeps a **paper checklist** and signs only after checking tax guidance.

steps.text: Check tax guidance before signing AI-assisted client explanations
Move thirty weekly into a rent and electricity buffer
Delay the new sofa for at least a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption — Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Alder Ledger to measure mistakes as well as speed. If AI handles first drafts and checks, the juniors must learn to spot the odd cases instead of just pressing send.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one could reduce the team before it reduces my own hours, because I catch the hard mismatches. Still, most of our paid work is thinking work, and a strong system could make the partners question even a team lead's wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd run a weekly review session where the juniors compare machine output with the source documents, and I'd record what fails. I would also ask the partners for a paid role developing the review process, while Sam and I keep saving thirty a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, but I want my hands on the tool rather than waiting for a notice. The pace at the desk would rise long before robots matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a junior whose work is taken first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Mara, the newest accountant, that I will teach her how to check a strange tax case. I cannot promise Mara (my junior accountant) a vacancy will stay open if someone leaves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the partners give you the extra work without extra pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show them the error log and ask for a salary review after three months. If they refuse, I'd look at remote accounting posts, because the local list is short.

say: I would ask Alder Ledger to count **errors** alongside speed.
I would help juniors learn **odd cases** before routine checking disappears.
think: The team could **shrink** before my own hours do.
My **lead wage** is still exposed because our paid work sits at a desk.
do: Run **weekly review** sessions using source documents and an error log.
Request a **paid process role** and a three-month salary review.
Search **remote posts** if extra review work brings no pay.
feel: She feels **anxious**, yet wants to shape the new review work.
S1.quote: I cannot promise Mara (my junior accountant) a vacancy will stay open if someone leaves.
fieldNote: She offers Mara practical **training** while refusing to promise a replacement vacancy.
She makes a **salary review** conditional on three months of logged errors, then considers remote work.

steps.text: Run weekly machine-output review sessions and log errors
Request paid review-process role and three-month salary review
Search remote accounting posts if extra review brings no pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 — Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the staff that full AGI in 2028 can do the thinking parts of our work, so we need an honest count of what clients will still buy. I would not tell Mara that being good guarantees a desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect Alder Ledger to lose the fees that pay our team, and Sam's shop work may stay hands-on until robots around 2031. That gives his work a little longer, but his irregular shifts cannot replace my salary if mine goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'd ask the partners for the fee split between routine returns and disputed work, then start looking for a salaried audit or compliance post that still exists. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2028, if our team hours are cut, I'd take a paid contract reviewing contested returns and keep applying for a salary; I cannot fund an unpaid reinvention.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm alarmed. Two weeks of savings is no runway for a profession whose main product just got cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend money on a new qualification now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if an employer offers paid study or a signed job subject to passing it. We have rent, and I won't sell Sam a course as if it were a guaranteed wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the robot date mean for your partner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam fits shop interiors by hand, so 2031 might threaten his shifts too. We would try to build three months of rent before then if paid work covers the bills, but my desk income is exposed in 2028.

say: I would ask what **clients still buy** when AGI can prepare returns in 2028.
I would tell the team that **skill alone** cannot guarantee a desk.
think: I expect **team fees** to fall, with my salary at risk in 2028.
Sam’s **hands-on work** may last until 2031, but irregular shifts cannot carry us.
do: Apply for **salaried audit** or compliance posts before 2028.
Take **paid contested-return** work if hours fall after AGI arrives.
Save toward **three months of rent** before 2031 if paid work covers current bills.
feel: She feels **alarmed** by two weeks of savings and two exposed incomes.
S2.quote: Two weeks of savings is no runway for a profession whose main product just got cheaper.
fieldNote: She clearly separates her **2028 desk risk** from Sam’s later hands-on robot exposure.
She refuses unfunded study and will take contested-return work only if **paid**.

steps.text: Apply for salaried audit or compliance vacancies before 2028
Take paid contested-return contracts if team hours fall after 2028
Save toward three months of rent before 2031 if paid work covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031 — Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years allows us to stop selling only annual returns. We could offer clients a clear explanation of their books each quarter, and test whether anyone pays for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2031 I could have a record of using AI well and a stronger savings buffer, but full AGI can still do the analysis I enjoy. Sam's hands-on work may hold until robots around 2034, yet we should not build our rent plan on those extra years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pitch a paid pilot to six existing small-business clients, with the partners' permission, and track the hours and fees. I would save thirty a week until we have three months of bills. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, I'd continue the service only if four of six clients renew at a fee covering staff hours; otherwise I'd apply for salaried compliance work beyond our town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, though I have time to test whether people pay for a human explanation. A free pilot would teach us nothing about our wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What number would make you continue the pilot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If four of the six pay for a second quarter at a fee covering our staff hours, I'd take that to the partners. If only one does, I would stop calling it a business line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for compliance work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam and I would consider a move for a written offer covering both our rent and the shifts he would lose. I would not move on the hope of an interview.

say: I would test a **paid quarterly** explanation service with six clients.
I would stop the pilot unless **four clients** buy a second quarter.
think: My **analysis work** stays exposed when AGI arrives in 2031.
Sam’s extra **three years** before robots will not pay the rent by themselves.
do: Pitch a **paid pilot** to six clients with the partners’ permission.
Save **thirty weekly** until three months of bills are covered.
Continue after **2031** only with four renewals covering staff hours; otherwise apply for salaried compliance work.
feel: She feels **anxious**, but has time to test whether clients will pay.
S3.quote: A free pilot would teach us nothing about our wages.
fieldNote: Her experiment has a clear **renewal threshold** and must cover staff hours, not just attract praise.
She would move only for a **written salary offer** that covers Sam’s lost shifts and the new rent.

steps.text: Pitch paid quarterly pilot to six clients with partners permission
Save thirty weekly until three months of bills are covered
Continue paid service after 2031 if four clients renew at covering fees
Apply for salaried compliance work if fewer than four clients renew

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036 — Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my colleagues we have ten years to learn what a client actually values, and to price that work. Waiting until 2036 would waste the best part of my career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 37 I'll still want paid work, but ten years lets me build something beyond signing routine returns. AGI still reaches my thinking work in 2036; Sam's shop-fitting faces robots around 2039, so both incomes need a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the partners' permission to lead accounts lessons for four clients next year, as salaried work at Alder Ledger; the client fees would go to the firm, not to me as second income. Sam and I would build six months of household bills in savings and consider a child only after that buffer and a full year of predictable income. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, if routine returns disappear, I'd keep the salaried lessons if the firm funds them and apply for posted, paid teaching jobs. I cannot assume a teaching vacancy will be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm uneasy, but less frightened than in 2028. Time gives us a way to earn evidence, save cash and make the family decision with open eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually teach an owner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to tell cash in the bank from profit, and which invoices are late enough to hurt wages. I'd charge for a short session and ask if the owner wants another one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as steady enough to plan a child?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Six months of bills saved and a full year of predictable income from both of us. Family should come before toys and a bigger flat, but I won't pretend a baby is free.

say: I would spend the **decade** pricing work clients value.
I would teach owners **cash versus profit** through paid short sessions.
think: At 37 my **desk work** is still exposed to AGI.
Sam’s **2039 robot risk** means both incomes need savings.
do: Launch **four-client lessons** as salaried Alder Ledger work with the partners’ permission.
Save **six months of bills** and wait for one predictable year before considering a child.
Apply for **posted paid teaching jobs** after 2036 if routine returns disappear.
feel: She feels **uneasy**, but hopes to test earnings over the decade.
S4.quote: Family should come before toys and a bigger flat, but I won't pretend a baby is free.
fieldNote: Her traditional **family priority** is tied to a clear cash and income threshold, not a vague wish.
She connects the **2036 desk deadline** with a later robot risk to Sam’s shop-fitting shifts.

steps.text: Launch paid accounts lessons with four clients with partners permission next year
Build six months of household expenses before family changes
Consider a child only after six months of bills saved and one year of predictable income
Apply for posted salaried teaching vacancies after 2036 if routine returns disappear

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 is the frightening one. I'd need a paid route into audit or compliance, a clear account of which Alder Ledger fees vanish, and enough rent saved to refuse a bad offer. I can learn quickly, but speed at learning does not pay the electricity bill.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what happens to the people who are still training. If Mara loses her first ladder rung, my team loses its next good reviewer too.

headlineQuote: I can learn quickly, but speed at learning does not pay the electricity bill.
portrait: Zoe, 27, leads accountants at **Alder Ledger** and holds a master’s degree plus a chartered qualification.
She is highly skilled and uses **AI daily**, checking tax sources before she signs client work.
Her pay is **low for the job**, Sam’s shop-fitting shifts vary, and the household has two weeks of expenses saved.
She tests **paid new services** and demands renewal evidence, while 2028 AGI threatens her desk income most.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove team fees before her household can build a useful rent buffer.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid path** into audit or compliance and clear information on lost fees would guide her next move.
